concept: High leverage short trading and risk of ruin
summary: Source-anchored research for High leverage short trading and risk of ruin. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: freqtrade is an open-source reference implementation of per-exchange liquidation formulas. Its Binance function uses the transcribed Binance formula with a tier rate and maintenance amount; its Bybit function uses the first-order form and refuses inverse contracts. Its documentation says it 'is able to calculate liquidation prices, but does not calculate liquidation fees', so liquidations 'will result in inaccurate profit/loss results for your bot', and cross-margin interactions may not be fully simulated. In backtests the Binance function falls back to each other trade's open rate where live runs use the mark price. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

A perpetual-futures short is a derivative position, not a loan of the asset. A long and a short counterparty agree a price without exchanging anything except margin posted with the venue; no underlying has to be acquired, so there is nothing to borrow or deliver; and the contract never expires. Because nothing forces convergence at maturity, a funding payment from one side to the other (peer-to-peer; Hyperliquid collects no fee on it) is the mechanism that pulls the perp price toward spot. (high confidence)

A stop set inside normal short-term price noise can be triggered and fill badly. SEC staff: a stop 'may be triggered by a short-term, intraday price move that results in an execution price for the stop order that is substantially worse', and brokers differ on whether last-sale or quotation prices trigger it. Hyperliquid builds its mark price from 'external CEX prices with Hyperliquid's book state', which it says is 'more robust than using a single instantaneous book price'. (medium confidence)

OKX does not publish a standalone futures liquidation price formula on the pages read. Its help page says position reduction or forced liquidation may be triggered when the maintenance margin ratio is at or below 100%, based on the mark price, and directs users to the built-in Futures Calculator (Liquidation Price tab). The calculator takes the pair, margin mode, direction, leverage, entry price, number of contracts and available margin. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-27)

On crypto venues a spot short is the same borrow-and-sell trade, funded from a lending pool whose price moves with conditions. Kraken says funds from its BTC margin pool let a client short sell, charges the fee on the quantity of the asset sold (its BTC example: 'could be 0.010%'), locks the rollover rate at order execution and states that margin rates fluctuate with market conditions. Aave's variable borrow rate is a two-slope function of pool utilization, with a second slope applying from the optimal usage ratio to 100 percent utilization, set per reserve. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-28)

Funding-rate arbitrage (long spot, short perp), the capital that takes the other side of leveraged long demand, is not risk-free. He et al.: it 'is not risk-free even disregarding margin requirements and trading costs, simply because there is no predetermined expiration date when the trade would be unwound at a profit', and temporary worsening of apparent arbitrage opportunities 'can lead to liquidations and losses'. BIS: engaging in cash-and-carry is risky because of spikes in margins and liquidations amid drawdowns. (high confidence)

The liquidation price a venue displays is an estimate and can move. Hyperliquid: the figure shown while entering a trade can differ because book liquidity changes, and after opening it can still differ because of funding payments or changes in unrealized PnL of other cross positions. OKX: 'the estimated liquidation price is not the actual price at which liquidation will occur', and in USDT cross-margin mode it cannot be calculated when the account holds two or more USDT futures or leveraged positions in different pairs. KuCoin: in cross margin, positions are liquidated only when the risk ratio reaches 100%, and the cross liquidation price is 'for reference only'. freqtrade: cross-margin effects between positions may not be fully simulated outside live trading. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Continuous-time Kelly for one risky asset with drift m, volatility s and risk-free rate r: f* = (m - r)/s^2, growth g(f) = r + f(m - r) - s^2 f^2 / 2 (an exact parabola in f), and maximum growth g(f*) = r + (m - r)^2 / (2 s^2) = r + S^2/2, where S is the Sharpe ratio. The fraction f is a multiple of equity, so f above 1 is leverage. Because f* x s = S, the Kelly-consistent annualised volatility target equals the Sharpe ratio. (high confidence)

Carver's translation of Kelly into a volatility target: with Gaussian returns the full-Kelly annualised risk target equals the expected Sharpe ratio (expected SR 0.5 means 50% annualised risk). He calls half Kelly 'a far safer bet', cut his own target to 25% a year ('closer to the 10 - 20% that most systematic trend following firms target'), and halves backtested performance as a rule of thumb because most backtests are overfitted. Thorp's identity f* x s = S gives the same result. (medium confidence)

ECB Financial Stability Review box (May 2020; the page gives only the month): a stylised four-asset risk-parity portfolio would have had to sell assets worth nearly 225% of its capital to meet its volatility target in March 2020, leaving a cash share near 25%. Estimates of money in volatility strategies run up to USD 2 trillion, including about USD 300 billion in some 100 risk-parity funds. The ECB says the model figures are not observed data and the contribution of these strategies to price moves 'remains hard to quantify'. (low confidence) (verified as of 2020-05-01)

Fixed-fractional sizing: choose the fraction of current equity to lose if the stop is hit, then size = equity x risk% / |entry - stop|. Kraken, Tapeboard and The Right Trader give this formula. Because the base is current equity, dollar risk grows with the account and shrinks after losses. Kraken: 'A common approach is to risk 0.5% to 2% of account per trade'; The Right Trader: the fraction is 'something you choose' and 'not a forecast', and 1% is 'a common retail choice, not a law'. (high confidence)

De-risk as drawdown grows. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba: practitioners who wish to protect capital above all 'sharply reduce risk as their drawdown increases'. The original Turtle rules, as reproduced on a blog, cut the notional account by 20% for each 10% drawdown, so position size shrank faster than equity. (medium confidence)

A correct perp short can still be force-closed by auto-deleveraging (ADL). When an account goes bankrupt and liquidators and the insurance fund cannot absorb it, venues close profitable opposite-side positions against it. Orderly: ADL fires only if liquidators do not take over, nobody claims the positions from the insurance fund, and the insurance fund margin ratio is below its minimum; it selects the traders with the most profit and the most leverage. Hyperliquid: opposite-side users are ranked by unrealized PnL and leverage and closed at the previous mark price against the underwater account. WuBlockchain's example is a crash where longs go bankrupt and the profitable shorts are cut. Campbell et al. define ADL as a rule-based way to spread losses across solvent participants. (high confidence)

ADL candidate ranking is venue-specific, so check the venue's docs before assuming who gets cut. Orderly ranks by profit and leverage; Hyperliquid sorts by (mark_price / entry_price) * (notional_position / account_value); Campbell et al. show that for single-asset isolated margin, reducing the highest-leverage accounts first (a 'minimax leverage' water-filling rule) is optimal for all monotone risk measures. (medium confidence)

A stop price is a trigger, not a guaranteed fill. SEC staff (equities): a stop order becomes a market order at the stop price, and its execution price 'can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the prices of available liquidity'; a stop-limit 'may not be executed if the stock's price moves away from the specified limit price'. The same failure shows on perps: Hyperliquid's FAQ says a long stop-loss with a $10 limit 'may rest at $10 without filling' if price drops from $11 to $9, and Mudrex says a skipped stop-limit can leave the position to be liquidated. (high confidence)

Hyperliquid's default slippage tolerance for market TP/SL orders is 10%. The limit price on a TP/SL order sets the slippage bound instead: a more aggressive limit makes a fill more likely but allows more slippage. In the docs' example, a long stop-loss triggered at $10 with a $10 limit may rest unfilled if price gaps down, while an $8 limit would likely fill between $9 and $8. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Pick the stop first, size from it, and treat leverage as an output. Kraken's sizing guide uses position size = (account value x risk %) / |entry - stop|, identical for shorts (stop above entry); leverage 'doesn't change the dollar risk if the stop is hit', and 'Never let your leverage setting determine how large a position you open'. Wealthsimple: 'The maximum leverage a platform allows is a limit, not a recommendation.' (medium confidence)

Liquidation triggers on a venue-defined reference price, not the last traded price. OKX: the liquidation price is based on the mark price, 'rather than the last price or the index price'. Hyperliquid: liquidations use a mark price that combines external CEX prices with Hyperliquid's book state. KuCoin: an isolated position enters liquidation when the mark price reaches the estimated liquidation price. dYdX: account value is estimated with the oracle price. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Volatility targeting sets exposure inversely to forecast volatility, so portfolio risk stays constant rather than notional exposure: leverage up when volatility is low, down when it is high. Moreira and Muir scale monthly returns by c divided by the previous month's realized variance (inverse-variance scaling); Harvey et al. scale by sigma_target divided by a volatility estimate known 24 hours ahead (inverse-volatility scaling), which they note has lower turnover than variance scaling. (high confidence)

A perp short carries basis risk that a borrow-and-sell short does not, because it is short the contract rather than the asset. He et al.: perpetuals 'are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price', and deviations from no-arbitrage prices in crypto are larger than in traditional currency markets (though they diminish over time). BIS researchers find 'excess volatility' of crypto futures relative to spot prices (a futures-wide finding, not perp-specific). (medium confidence)

Auto-deleveraging (ADL) can close winning shorts. Hyperliquid: if an account's value or isolated position value goes negative, opposite-side users are ranked by unrealized PnL and leverage using (mark_price / entry_price) x (notional_position / account_value), and are closed at the previous mark price. FTI: on 2025-10-10 'some of the best-hedged shorts found their positions reduced or entirely closed', which can turn a hedged portfolio into a naked one. BitMEX: ADL across multiple exchanges disrupted delta-neutral strategies, forced professional market makers to cut liquidity, and left order books at their thinnest since 2022. (high confidence)

Inference from the tier rules: a short's notional rises as the price rises, so a large short can move into a higher-rate tier before it reaches the liquidation price that a flat-rate formula gives. A long's notional falls as its price falls, so the same tier effect works in its favour. Hyperliquid solves for the tier at the liquidation price; a flat-rate calculator does not, and so can overstate a large short's cushion. (medium confidence)

Kelly sizing maximizes the expected log of wealth, which maximizes the limiting exponential growth rate of wealth. Thorp's Theorem 1: if the per-bet growth rate g(f) is above zero, wealth tends to infinity almost surely; if g(f) is below zero, wealth tends to zero almost surely (ruin is almost sure); at g(f) = 0 wealth oscillates between 0 and infinity. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba name the main drawback: the suggested wagers can be very large, so Kelly is very risky in the short term. (high confidence)
